newsitem.title: THAILAND: Lull seen for Thailand as speculators lick wounds.
newsitem.headline: Lull seen for Thailand as speculators lick wounds.

text.p: Thailand, stung last week by a fierce speculative attack on its currency, should be in for a calmer ride this week as speculators who lost take time off to lick their wounds and recuperate, analysts said.
Speculators who raided the baht were severely bruised when the Bank of Thailand, joined by counterparts in the region, hit back with a coordinated defence and choked adventurous punters.

Dealers and economists said speculators lost vast amounts of money as the central bank cut them off from cheap sources of short-term funds and made it more expensive to buy back the baht they had driven down so sharply to make later gains.
Although speculators could lay off the baht for a while, there was always a chance they could return to haunt Thailand in the future when it exposed any vulnerability, they said.

"In the short term I don't think anything will happen in Thailand. This time the central bank won. But don't forget, the speculators got knocked down but they are not dead," said Firdosh Bathena, senior vice president at Asia Credit Plc.

Thailand's weak economy, with growth seen slowing to a 10-year-low of around five percent, sluggish exports, high interest rates and ailing finance and property sectors have made it attractive prey for speculative attacks, analysts said.
The baht, fixed daily by the central bank against a basket of currencies heavily weighted in the dollar, was the target of similar attacks in February and late last year.

Analysts said Thailand needed to take speedy measures to cut interest rates, now among the highest in the region at 12.75-13.00 percent, to give the economy a boost and enable cash-strapped businesses breathing room.
Urgent reform of the Thai currency system to make the baht more flexible would help fend off speculators, analysts said.

"Time is running out for the Thai policy makers. They are in some sense pressured to make some kind of major changes after this," said Ng Bok Eng, regional economist at Singapore-based Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"A quick firm decision on currency reform is needed. They certainly need a more flexible baht policy," he added.
Others said the central bank was aware of the need for currency reform but was against being pressured by other quarters, especially speculators, into making changes.
But a dealer at Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corp cautioned that it was premature to think that Thailand or other regional central banks had won the war against speculators.
"On the surface, the baht is riding on calmer waters but I still think it is premature to say Thailand has won the war," he said.

"The professional speculators who the Bank of Thailand has dealt with this week are diehard people who, I suspect, will now wait on the sidelines for a new opportunity to pounce on the baht when Thailand stumbles or its economy shows new signs of weakness," he added.
The immediate future for Thailand, its currency and the sagging stock market also hinged on the way top government officials and bureaucrats conducted themselves, analysts said.

"They all talk too much and divergently as well. This causes confusion among investors, especially foreign investors, and Thailand becomes viewed as a basket case," said an analyst at a local brokerage who declined to be identified.

As the run on the baht raged last week, a senior advisor to the Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh criticised Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan, signalling there was dissent within the government, analysts said.
A major political party in Chavalit's six-party administration engineered behind-the-scenes action to discredit Amnuay while the baht was embattled, they added.
Amnuay, whom the premier later said he fully supported, was put in an awkward position, making matters worse for Thailand's already tattered image abroad, they said.
